\textbf{1} Express the following as trigonometric ratios of either $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ or $60^\circ$, and hence find their exact values.\quad
\textbf{a } $\sin135^\circ$\quad\textbf{b } $\sin(-60^\circ)$\quad\textbf{c } $\sin330^\circ$\quad\textbf{d } $\sin420^\circ$\quad\textbf{e } $\sin(-300^\circ)$\quad\textbf{f } $\cos120^\circ$\quad\textbf{g } $\cos300^\circ$\quad\textbf{h } $\cos225^\circ$\quad\textbf{i } $\cos(-210^\circ)$\quad\textbf{j } $\cos495^\circ$\quad\textbf{k } $\tan135^\circ$\quad\textbf{l } $\tan(-225^\circ)$\quad\textbf{m } $\tan210^\circ$\quad\textbf{n } $\tan300^\circ$\quad\textbf{o } $\tan(-120^\circ)$.

\textbf{a } $\sin135^\circ=+\sin45^\circ$ ($135^\circ$ is in the second quadrant at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\sin135^\circ=\frac{\sqrt2}2$.
\textbf{b } $\sin(-60^\circ)=-\sin60^\circ$ ($-60^\circ$ is in the fourth quadrant at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\sin(-60^\circ)=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
\textbf{c } $\sin330^\circ=-\sin30^\circ$ ($330^\circ$ is in the fourth quadrant at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\sin330^\circ=-\frac12$.
\textbf{d } $\sin420^\circ=+\sin60^\circ$ (on second revolution). So $\sin420^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.

\textbf{e } $\sin(-300^\circ)=+\sin60^\circ$ ($-300^\circ$ is in the first quadrant at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\sin(-300^\circ)=\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
\textbf{f } $\cos120^\circ=-\cos60^\circ$ ($120^\circ$ is in the second quadrant at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\cos120^\circ=-\frac12$.
\textbf{g } $\cos300^\circ=+\cos60^\circ$ ($300^\circ$ is in the fourth quadrant at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\cos300^\circ=\frac12$.
\textbf{h } $\cos225^\circ=-\cos45^\circ$ ($225^\circ$ is in the third quadrant at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\cos225^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt2}2$.

\textbf{i } $\cos(-210^\circ)=-\cos30^\circ$ ($-210^\circ$ is in the second quadrant at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\cos(-210^\circ)=-\frac{\sqrt3}2$.
\textbf{j } $\cos495^\circ=-\cos45^\circ$ ($495^\circ$ is in the second quadrant at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\cos495^\circ=-\frac{\sqrt2}2$.
\textbf{k } $\tan135^\circ=-\tan45^\circ$ ($135^\circ$ is in the second quadrant at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\tan135^\circ=-1$.
\textbf{l } $\tan(-225^\circ)=-\tan45^\circ$ ($-225^\circ$ is in the second quadrant at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\tan(-225^\circ)=-1$.

\textbf{m } $\tan210^\circ=+\tan30^\circ$ ($210^\circ$ is in the third quadrant at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\tan210^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}3$.
\textbf{n } $\tan300^\circ=-\tan60^\circ$ ($300^\circ$ is in the fourth quadrant at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\tan300^\circ=-\sqrt3$.
\textbf{o } $\tan(-120^\circ)=+\tan60^\circ$ ($-120^\circ$ is in the third quadrant at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal.) So $\tan(-120^\circ)=\sqrt3$.

\begin{array}{lll}
\cos^{-1}(-0.4)=113.58\ (\alpha)&\text{Awrt 114}&B1\\

&\text{Allow }x=\frac{\alpha\pm10}3\text{ not }\frac\alpha3\pm10&\\

Note: If $x=\frac{\alpha\pm10}3$ is not clearly applied from the first angle it may be recovered if applied to the second or third angle.
\textbf{Note 1:} Do not penalise incorrect accuracy more than once and penalise it the first time it occurs. E.g if answers are only given to the nearest integer (41, 85, 161) only the first A mark that would otherwise be scored is lost.
\textbf{Note 2:} Ignore any answers outside the range. For extra answers in range in an otherwise fully correct solution lose final A1.
\textbf{Note 3:} Lack of working means that it is sometimes not clear where their intermediate angles are coming from. In these cases, if the final answers are incorrect score M0.
\textbf{Note 4:} Candidates are unlikely to be working in radians deliberately but may have their calculator in radian mode (gives $\alpha=1.98$). In such cases the main scheme should be applied and the method marks are available. \textbf{4} Solve for $0\le x\le180^\circ$ the equations:
\textbf{a} $\sin(x+20^\circ)=\frac12$.

\textbf{5 a} Sketch for $0\le x\le360^\circ$ the graph of $y=\sin(x+60^\circ)$.
\textbf{b} Write down the exact coordinates of the points where the graph meets the coordinate axes.
\textbf{c} Solve, for $0\le x\le360^\circ$, the equation $\sin(x+60^\circ)=0.55$, giving your answers to 1 decimal place.

\textbf{a} Let $X=x+20^\circ$. So $\sin X=\frac12$. As $X=x+20^\circ$, then as $0\le x\le180^\circ$, so $0+20\le x\le180^\circ+20$. So the interval for $X$ is $20^\circ\le X\le200^\circ$.
$X=30^\circ,150^\circ$, i.e. $x+20^\circ=30^\circ,150^\circ$. So $x=10^\circ,130^\circ$.

\textbf{b} Let $X=2x$. So $\cos X=-0.8$. As $X=2x$, then as $0\le x\le180^\circ$, so $2\times0\le X\le2\times180^\circ$. So the interval for $X$ is $0\le X\le360^\circ$.
$X=143.13^\circ,216.87^\circ$, i.e. $2x=143.13^\circ,216.87^\circ$. So $x=71.6^\circ,108.4^\circ$.

\textbf{c} Let $X=x+60^\circ$. So $\sin X=0.55$. As $X=x+60^\circ$, then as $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$, so $0^\circ+60\le x\le360^\circ+60$. So the interval for $X$ is $60^\circ\le X\le420^\circ$.
$X=33.4^\circ,146.6^\circ,393.4^\circ$, i.e. $x+60^\circ=33.4^\circ,146.6^\circ,393.4^\circ$. So $x=86.6^\circ,333.4^\circ$.

\textbf{b} State, with justification, whether this is the only such possible value of $k$.
\textbf{a}\quad $4\sin x=3\cos x$, $\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=\dfrac34$, $\tan x=\dfrac34$.

\textbf{b} Let $X=2\theta$. So $\tan X=\frac34$. As $X=2\theta$, then as $0^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$, so $2\times0^\circ\le X\le2\times360^\circ$. So the interval for $X$ is $0^\circ\le X\le720^\circ$.
$X=36.87^\circ,216.87^\circ,396.87^\circ,576.87^\circ$, i.e. $2\theta=36.87^\circ,216.87^\circ,396.87^\circ,576.87^\circ$. So $\theta=18.4^\circ,108.4^\circ,198.4^\circ,288.4^\circ$.

\textbf{b} No because when $X=330^\circ$, $k=5.5$. As $k$ increases, the period of the tan graph increases.

\textbf{(a)} Show that the equation $5\sin x=1+2\cos^2x$ can be written in the form $2\sin^2x+5\sin x-3=0$. (2)
\textbf{(b)} Solve, for $0\le x<360^\circ$, $2\sin^2x+5\sin x-3=0$. (4)

\textbf{(a)} $5\sin x=1+2(1-\sin^2x)$ (M1). $2\sin^2x+5\sin x-3=0\quad(*)$ (A1cso, 2).
\textbf{(b)} $(2s-1)(s+3)=0$ giving $s=$ (M1).

\textbf{5} Find all the solutions, in the interval $0\le x\le360^\circ$, to the equation $8\sin^2x+6\cos x-9=0$ giving each solution to one decimal place. (6 marks)
\textbf{6} Find, for $0\le x\le360^\circ$, all the solutions of $\sin^2x+1=\frac72\cos^2x$ giving each solution to one decimal place.

$8\sin^2x+6\cos x-9=0$ can be written as $8(1-\cos^2x)+6\cos x-9=0$ which reduces to $8\cos^2x-6\cos x+1=0$. So $(4\cos x-1)(2\cos x-1)=0$, $\cos x=\frac14$ or $\cos x=\frac12$. So $x=75.5^\circ,284.5^\circ,60^\circ,300^\circ$.
The solutions are $x=60^\circ,75.5^\circ,284.5^\circ,300^\circ$.
$\sin^2x+1=\frac72\cos^2x$ can be written as $\sin^2x+1=\frac72(1-\sin^2x)$. $2\sin^2x+2=7-7\sin^2x$ which reduces to $9\sin^2x-5=0$. $\sin^2x=\frac59$, $\sin x=\pm\frac{\sqrt5}3$.
\textbf{7} Show that the equation $2\cos^2x+\cos x-6=0$ has no solutions.
\textbf{8 a} Show that the equation $\cos^2x=2-\sin x$ can be written as $\sin^2x-\sin x+1=0$. (2 marks)
\textbf{b} Hence show that the equation $\cos^2x=2-\sin x$ has no solutions. (3 marks)
$2\cos^2x+\cos x-6=0$, $(2\cos x-3)(\cos x+2)=0$, $\cos x=\frac32$ or $\cos x=-2$. There are no solutions to $\cos x=\frac32$ or $\cos x=-2$, so the equation has no solutions.
\textbf{a} $\cos^2x=2-\sin x$ can be written as $(1-\sin^2x)=2-\sin x$, $\sin^2x-\sin x+1=0$.
\textbf{b}\quad $\sin^2x-\sin x+1=0$. Using the discriminant $b^2-4ac=(-1)^2-4\times1\times1$
As $b^2-4ac<0$, therefore there are no real roots.

\textbf{9}\quad $\tan^2x-2\tan x-4=0$.
\textbf{a} Show that $\tan x=p\pm\sqrt q$ where $p$ and $q$ are numbers to be found.
\textbf{b} Hence solve the equation $\tan^2x-2\tan x-4=0$ in the interval $0\le x\le540^\circ$.
\textbf{a}\quad $\tan^2x-2\tan x-4=0$,\[\tan x=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{(-2)^2-4(1)(-4)}}{2(1)}=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{20}}2=\frac{2\pm2\sqrt5}2=1\pm\sqrt5.\] $p=1,\ q=5$.

\textbf{b}\quad $\tan x=1\pm\sqrt5$, $x=72.8^\circ,252.8^\circ,432.8^\circ,-51.0^\circ,129.0^\circ,309.0^\circ,489.0^\circ$. So the solutions are $x=72.8^\circ,129.0^\circ,252.8^\circ,309.0^\circ,432.8^\circ,489.0^\circ$.
